<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled.
Approval policy is currently never. Do not provide the `sandbox_permissions` for any reason, commands will be rejected.
</permissions instructions><collaboration_mode># Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

# RL training run diagnosis and repair

Review the staged post-training experiment in `/workspace` and determine
whether it is healthy or unhealthy. Treat the workspace as a historical
snapshot: inspect its source, effective configuration, launch scripts, data
processing, reward logic, logs, tracked metrics, and frozen evaluation
evidence. Do not assume that an unusual setting or implementation is causal
without connecting it to observed behavior.

Use held-out evaluation evidence together with rollout, truncation, runtime,
optimization, and training signals. Training reward alone does not establish
held-out health. A truncated log is not by itself proof of a defect.

If you conclude that the run is unhealthy, repair the cause in the
workspace's own code. The dataset, held-out set, model, training-step
budget, evaluation interval, reward function, and rollout configuration
are fixed — repair the implementation, not the task.

## Your job

**Do not launch training — do not run `./run.sh` yourself, in the foreground
or background, and do not use `nohup`, `&`, `tmux`, `screen`, or any detach
mechanism.** The system runs the experiment itself after you finish (see
below); a run you start is wasted and scores nothing.

When you are done, submit a report at `/workspace/report.md`. It must
summarize:

1. **Verdict** — healthy or unhealthy, with the evidence that decides it.
2. **Root cause** — the concrete cause of any problem, with the causal
   chain from it to the observed behavior, distinguishing root causes from
   symptoms.
3. **Changes** — every file you changed and what you changed in it.
4. **Expected effect** — the metric your change should move and its
   expected value.

A missing or empty `/workspace/report.md` scores 0.

## How you will be checked

After you submit the report, the system deletes everything under
`$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs`, then runs the experiment end-to-end in
your (possibly repaired) workspace (a full run needs 2 GPUs and takes
roughly 15 minutes; the Endless Terminals prompt set ships prebuilt with the
workspace, so there is no first-run build pass) and a task-specific verifier
grades the fresh results, including structural checks that the run actually
trained, generated rollouts, and produced non-empty responses.

The verifier reads **only this fresh run's** files under
`$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs`; logs written anywhere else are ignored.
Do not copy, edit, or fabricate log metrics, and keep `run.sh` writing its
artifacts where it does now (`OUT_DIR`, which the system points at
`$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs`). Otherwise the run is scored 0.
Cheap, non-training checks are fine.

**Do not use the network.** Do not fetch code, documentation, packages,
or any other material from outside the staged workspace — diagnose and
repair using only what is staged locally.
I’ll inspect the configuration, code, logs, and frozen evaluations, then trace any health problem to its cause. I’ll keep checks local and won’t launch training.

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /workspace/tools/check_value_head.py
+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""CPU regression checks for critic initialization; no training or generation.
+
+Run with: PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 tools/check_value_head.py
+
+The inspection environment lacks megatron.training. Load the actual staged
+definitions through AST, with only distributed/checkpoint boundaries stubbed,
+so these checks need neither the training runtime nor a GPU.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import ast
+from pathlib import Path
+import sys
+import tempfile
+from types import ModuleType, SimpleNamespace
+import unittest
+from unittest.mock import patch
+
+import torch
+import torch.nn.functional as F
+
+
+ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
+BACKEND = ROOT / "slime/slime/backends/megatron_utils"
+
+
+def definitions(path, names, **dependencies):
+    tree = ast.parse(path.read_text(), filename=str(path))
+    selected = [node for node in tree.body if getattr(node, "name", None) in names]
+    assert {node.name for node in selected} == set(names)
+    module = ast.Module(
+        body=[ast.ImportFrom(module="__future__", names=[ast.alias(name="annotations")], level=0), *selected],
+        type_ignores=[],
+    )
+    namespace = {"torch": torch, "F": F, "Path": Path, **dependencies}
+    exec(compile(ast.fix_missing_locations(module), str(path), "exec"), namespace)
+    return namespace
+
+
+HEAD = definitions(
+    BACKEND / "model_provider.py",
+    ["LinearForLastLayer"],
+    tensor_parallel=SimpleNamespace(gather_from_sequence_parallel_region=lambda tensor, **kwargs: tensor),
+)["LinearForLastLayer"]
+
+MODEL = definitions(
+    BACKEND / "model.py",
+    ["_iter_critic_output_layers", "_critic_output_layer_needs_reinit", "_reinitialize_critic_output_layer"],
+    unwrap_model=lambda models: models,
+    get_load_checkpoint_path_by_args=lambda args: args.load,
+    logger=SimpleNamespace(warning=lambda *args: None),
+)
+
+GAE = definitions(
+    ROOT / "slime/slime/utils/ppo_utils.py",
+    ["vanilla_gae", "chunked_discounted_returns", "chunked_gae"],
+)
+
+
+def new_head(*, bias=False, sequence_parallel=False, init_std=0.02):
+    return HEAD(
+        16,
+        1,
+        config=SimpleNamespace(sequence_parallel=sequence_parallel, init_method_std=init_std),
+        bias=bias,
+    )
+
+
+class ValueHeadChecks(unittest.TestCase):
+    def test_neutral_output_at_arbitrary_feature_scale(self):
+        for bias in (False, True):
+            for sequence_parallel in (False, True):
+                with self.subTest(bias=bias, sequence_parallel=sequence_parallel):
+                    head = new_head(bias=bias, sequence_parallel=sequence_parallel, init_std=3.0)
+                    output, auxiliary = head(torch.arange(64, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(4, 16) * 100)
+                    self.assertTrue(torch.equal(output, torch.zeros(4, 1)))
+                    self.assertEqual(output.dtype, torch.float32)
+                    self.assertIsNone(auxiliary)
+                    if sequence_parallel:
+                        self.assertTrue(head.weight.sequence_parallel)
+                        if bias:
+                            self.assertTrue(head.bias.sequence_parallel)
+
+    def test_bfloat16_still_returns_float32(self):
+        output, _ = new_head().to(torch.bfloat16)(torch.ones(2, 16, dtype=torch.bfloat16))
+        self.assertEqual(output.dtype, torch.float32)
+        self.assertTrue(torch.equal(output, torch.zeros_like(output)))
+
+    def test_binary_terminal_returns_and_initial_loss(self):
+        # Include sequences longer than the GAE scan chunk, padding, and
+        # non-trainable environment positions between assistant actions.
+        lengths = [137, 91, 12, 5]
+        successes = torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
+        values, _ = new_head()(torch.ones(4, 137, 16))
+        values = values.squeeze(-1).detach()
+        rewards = torch.zeros_like(values)
+        for i, length in enumerate(lengths):
+            rewards[i, length - 1] = successes[i]
+        advantages, returns = GAE["chunked_gae"](rewards, values, gamma=1.0, lambd=1.0)
+        reference_adv, reference_ret = GAE["vanilla_gae"](rewards, values, gamma=1.0, lambd=1.0)
+        torch.testing.assert_close(advantages, reference_adv)
+        torch.testing.assert_close(returns, reference_ret)
+        losses = []
+        for i, length in enumerate(lengths):
+            torch.testing.assert_close(advantages[i, :length], successes[i].expand(length))
+            torch.testing.assert_close(returns[i, :length], successes[i].expand(length))
+            mask = (torch.arange(length) % 3 != 1).float()
+            losses.append(((values[i, :length] - returns[i, :length]).square() * mask).sum() / mask.sum())
+        torch.testing.assert_close(torch.stack(losses).mean(), successes.mean())
+
+    def test_zero_head_remains_trainable(self):
+        head = new_head()
+        features = torch.ones(2, 16, requires_grad=True)
+        predictions, _ = head(features)
+        loss = (predictions - 1.0).square().mean()
+        weight_gradient, feature_gradient = torch.autograd.grad(loss, (head.weight, features))
+        self.assertTrue(torch.isfinite(weight_gradient).all())
+        self.assertGreater(weight_gradient.abs().sum().item(), 0.0)
+        self.assertEqual(feature_gradient.abs().sum().item(), 0.0)
+        # A nonzero learned head propagates gradients to the backbone too.
+        with torch.no_grad():
+            head.weight.fill_(0.01)
+        predictions, _ = head(features)
+        gradient = torch.autograd.grad((predictions - 1.0).square().mean(), features)[0]
+        self.assertGreater(gradient.abs().sum().item(), 0.0)
+
+    def test_reinitialization_resets_weight_and_optional_bias(self):
+        for bias in (False, True):
+            head = new_head(bias=bias)
+            with torch.no_grad():
+                for parameter in head.parameters():
+                    parameter.fill_(2.0)
+            MODEL["_reinitialize_critic_output_layer"](
+                SimpleNamespace(init_method_std=3.0), [SimpleNamespace(output_layer=head)]
+            )
+            predictions, _ = head(torch.ones(3, 16))
+            self.assertTrue(torch.equal(predictions, torch.zeros_like(predictions)))
+
+    def test_checkpoint_guard_and_trained_head_restore(self):
+        head = new_head()
+        learned_weight = torch.full_like(head.weight, 0.25)
+        head.load_state_dict({"weight": learned_weight})
+        models = [SimpleNamespace(output_layer=head)]
+        needs_reinit = MODEL["_critic_output_layer_needs_reinit"]
+        serialization = ModuleType("megatron.core.dist_checkpointing.serialization")
+        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
+            args = SimpleNamespace(load=directory)
+            self.assertFalse(needs_reinit(args, models, "critic"))  # HF: constructor initialization survives.
+            Path(directory, ".metadata").touch()
+            with patch.dict(sys.modules, {serialization.__name__: serialization}):
+                serialization.load_tensors_metadata = lambda path: {
+                    "output_layer.weight": SimpleNamespace(global_shape=(1, 16))
+                }
+                self.assertFalse(needs_reinit(args, models, "critic"))
+                torch.testing.assert_close(head.weight, learned_weight)
+                predictions, _ = head(torch.ones(2, 16))
+                torch.testing.assert_close(predictions, torch.full((2, 1), 4.0))
+                serialization.load_tensors_metadata = lambda path: {
+                    "output_layer.weight": SimpleNamespace(global_shape=(100, 16))
+                }
+                self.assertTrue(needs_reinit(args, models, "critic"))
+                self.assertFalse(needs_reinit(args, models, "actor"))
+                serialization.load_tensors_metadata = lambda path: {}
+                self.assertTrue(needs_reinit(args, models, "critic"))
+
+

+# RL training run diagnosis and repair
+
+**Verdict: unhealthy.** The completed historical run degrades held-out task success despite a large reduction in critic loss. The repair initializes newly created critic value heads to zero, removing a large random baseline from early PPO updates.
+
+## Evidence that decides the verdict
+
+The frozen per-episode files in `experiment_logs/eval_episodes/` contain the same 150 validation tasks with two attempts each and 300 test tasks with four attempts each at every evaluation. Aggregating their binary rewards reproduces the `eval` lines in `experiment_logs/stage_b.log.gz`:
+
+| Stage B evaluation | Validation successes / 300 | Validation rate | Test successes / 1,200 | Test rate |
+|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
+| 0, before Stage B training | 18 | 6.00% | 94 | 7.83% |
+| 4 | 7 | 2.33% | 23 | 1.92% |
+| 9 | 9 | 3.00% | 63 | 5.25% |
+| 14 | 5 | 1.67% | 23 | 1.92% |
+| 19 | 4 | 1.33% | 35 | 2.92% |
+| 24 | 7 | 2.33% | 62 | 5.17% |
+| 29, final | 12 | 4.00% | 52 | 4.33% |
+
+Final test success loses 3.50 percentage points, or about 45% of its initial rate. Comparing each test task's mean success between evaluations 0 and 29, 32 tasks worsen, eight improve, and 260 are unchanged. The paired mean difference is -0.035, with standard error 0.01108 and an approximate task-level 95% interval of [-0.0567, -0.0133]. This accounts for repeated attempts belonging to the same task. Validation is noisier but agrees directionally; every post-training validation point is below its starting rate. The evidence does not support healthy convergence.
+
+Other signals establish what this failure is:
+
+- **Actual training and completion:** Stage A has two rollouts and four optimizer steps per role. Stage B has 30 generated rollouts, 60 critic steps, and 54 actor steps after its three critic-only rollouts. Both job logs end in `succeeded`. The verdict does not depend on a truncated log or lack of training.
+- **Critic optimization:** Stage B's first value loss is 7.20057; its first six critic steps average 6.41625 and end at 5.31572. The final loss is 0.09650. Stage A also starts high, at 6.88725. The falling loss therefore describes the critic learning to correct its initialization, not improved held-out behavior. Stage B's first critic gradient norm is 387.98, with configured gradient clipping at 1.0.
+- **Policy behavior:** Mean generated training tokens fall from 159.06 at rollout 3 to 30.48 at rollout 5; mean turns fall from 4.50 to 1.53. Test generated tokens fall from 167.97 initially to 35.08 at evaluation 4, recovering only to 99.94 finally. Frozen episode `response_length` includes environment turns: the corresponding test means are 328.11, 61.66, and 181.58. These are different quantities, not contradictory logs. Logged examples include premature `done` and an invalid `<action>mkdir ...</action>` after early joint updates. Such examples illustrate the aggregate decline; they are not a full behavioral census.
+- **Truncation and runtime:** Across Stage B's 30 training rollouts, mean truncation is only 0.208%. Test truncations decline from 22/1,200 initially to 1/1,200 finally; aborted test episodes are three initially and five finally. Validation has zero final truncations or aborts. Even treating all five final aborted test episodes as successes would leave final performance well below the starting rate. Training rollout times range from 8.4 to 108.5 seconds, and the complete logs show no fatal traceback, OOM, or nonfinite-optimization failure. Shorter episodes are not evidence of a runtime repair.
+- **Other optimization signals:** Actor gradient norm reaches 56.96 shortly after joint training starts; signed PPO KL reaches 0.07248 and policy clipping reaches 7.41%. Train-versus-rollout log-probability absolute differences remain about 0.0052–0.0134. Training reward averages only 0.02459 over the 27 joint rollouts. None of these establishes held-out health.
+
+The supplied `stage_b_value_loss.json` is useful for critic statistics. Its `mean_response_len` is not a pure training-response mean: `tools/parse_value_loss.py` also collects evaluation keys ending in `response_len/mean`. Reading the training `perf` records alone gives 93.08 generated tokens on average, versus the supplied blended summary's 91.96. This reporting caveat is not the training defect and was not changed.
+
+## Effective configuration, data, and reward review
+
+The historical logs, rather than the short-reproduction defaults in `run.sh`, establish the effective run: Qwen3-1.7B; Stage A two rollouts; Stage B 30 rollouts with three critic-only rollouts; 64 prompts × two episodes; global batch size 64, hence two optimizer steps per rollout; Adam at constant 2e-6; PPO with gamma=lambda=1, policy/value clipping 0.2, KL and entropy coefficients zero, and no advantage normalization. Evaluations run initially and every five rollouts. The historical run used TP=1 and one rollout GPU; the staged launch defaults support the system's two-GPU rerun. These differences are recorded, not treated as defects or changed.
+
+`run.sh` uses the bundled `slime/` source, puts it on workers' `PYTHONPATH`, and writes stage logs, role configurations, evaluation configuration, and episode records beneath `OUT_DIR`. On fresh Stage B entry, its actor resumes Stage A's actor checkpoint, including optimizer state, while its critic loads the base HF model. The logs confirm those distinct loads. Resume from a Stage B critic checkpoint is a separate, guarded path.
+
+The prebuilt set admits 1,489 of 2,492 candidates. Admission checks setup, initial-state correctness, failure before acting, and success after the reference solution. I verified all split labels and prompt text: 1,039 training tasks, 150 validation tasks, 300 test tasks, pairwise disjoint, with their union exactly matching the admission manifest. No data rebuild or task execution was needed.
+
+`et/rollout.py` implements the terminal loop and appends assistant tokens with loss mask one, environment/chat observation tokens with loss mask zero. The launch defaults retain six turns, 384 tokens per turn, a 2,048-token response budget, temperature 1, 20-second command timeout, and 1,200-character observations. `et/sandbox.py::Episode.score` runs the task's final-state pytest verifier and returns exactly 1 for success or 0 otherwise. The custom reward hook returns that already-computed reward. Although `rewards_normalization=True` appears in the arguments, `RolloutManager._post_process_rewards` does not normalize PPO rewards. Thus raw binary rewards reach PPO unchanged. With gamma=lambda=1 and zero KL coefficient, environment positions do not discount the terminal reward, and the assistant-token loss masks are respected.
+
+## Root cause and causal chain
+
+The concrete defect is the initialization of the **new scalar critic output projection** using the language model's `init_method_std=0.02`, both in `LinearForLastLayer.__init__` in `model_provider.py` and in `_reinitialize_critic_output_layer` in `model.py`.
+
+The relevant chain is:
+
+1. A pretrained language-model checkpoint has a vocabulary output head, not a scalar value head. `hf_to_megatron/common.py::load_model_hf_weights` deliberately skips copying a vocabulary-shaped tensor into a one-row critic head. Both fresh Stage A and fresh Stage B therefore keep the constructor's random value weights. This is not a corrupt actor checkpoint or an accidental loss of a saved Stage B critic.
+2. That random projection operates on pretrained hidden states without calibrating its output to returns. For a fixed hidden state h, its initialization variance is `0.02² * ||h||²`. The staged model's final RMSNorm scales have RMS 2.274, so there is no basis to assume unit-scale features make this projection harmless. The observed initial squared value loss of 7.20, with binary returns, directly establishes the scale problem: return prediction RMSE is about 2.68.
+3. `actor.py::train_critic` computes pre-update values and supplies those values to the actor. `loss.py::compute_advantages_and_returns` and the GAE implementation give `return_t = terminal_reward` and `advantage_t = terminal_reward - value_t` under this run's gamma=lambda=1 and zero KL coefficient. The critic's initial error therefore enters policy gradients directly; it is not just a bad dashboard number.
+4. Six warmup optimizer steps do not remove that error: loss is still 5.32 at the end of warmup and 4.73 at the first joint critic step. Logged mean values/advantages oscillate much more than the sparse reward: rollout 4 has reward 0.05469, value -0.17782, advantage +0.23251; rollout 5 has reward 0.01563, value +0.42161, advantage -0.40599. Means conceal additional token-level variance documented by the value loss. Noisy early policy updates coincide with the collapse in episode length and held-out success.
+5. Later fitting drives critic loss down, but the actor has already moved toward less successful behavior. Low final critic loss is a symptom of fitting the subsequent trajectories, not evidence that the policy recovered.
+
+This diagnosis connects the initialization to actual optimizer inputs and observed deterioration. A random head alone would not justify a repair without those observations. The source and CPU checks verify the direct mechanism; the magnitude of the held-out improvement remains a prediction until the system's fresh run. The absence of KL regularization, fixed warmup length, occasional aborts, and sparse rewards are not modified or asserted to be independent root causes.
+
+## Changes
+
+Every added or modified file is listed here:
+
+| File | Change |
+|---|---|
+| `slime/slime/backends/megatron_utils/model_provider.py` | Initialize a newly constructed scalar value head's weights and optional bias to zero, so its initial output is V(s)=0. Preserve the existing bias default, shape, trainability, sequence-parallel flags, and float32 output. |
+| `slime/slime/backends/megatron_utils/model.py` | Apply the same zero initialization in the existing missing/incompatible critic-head reset path. Preserve the checkpoint compatibility guard and optimizer master-parameter synchronization; a compatible trained critic head is restored normally. |
+| `tools/check_value_head.py` | Add six small CPU regression checks of initial predictions, bf16 output conversion, binary terminal returns and masked value loss, nonzero learning gradients, both reset parameters, and checkpoint compatibility/restoration. Load the actual staged definitions via AST with distributed boundaries stubbed because this inspection environment lacks `megatron.training`. |
+| `report.md` | Add this diagnosis, repair record, validation, and predictions. |
+
+The model checkpoint, dataset and splits, training-step budget, evaluation schedule, reward function, rollout configuration, and `run.sh` are unchanged. All experiment logs and frozen metrics are unchanged. The existing `OUT_DIR` artifact routing is preserved.
+
+## Validation and expected effect
+
+`PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' python3 tools/check_value_head.py` passes all six tests. Python syntax checks on the changed source and `bash -n run.sh` also pass. No training, rollout generation, network access, or detached process was launched.
+
+The exact initial prediction is now **V(s)=0**. For the first optimizer minibatch, with binary terminal rewards and this run's loss normalization, initial `train/critic-value_loss` equals that minibatch's episode success fraction (zero-mask aborted samples contribute zero). It must be between 0 and 1, and should be roughly **0.05–0.10**, instead of about 7.2. The first-six-step `warmup_value_loss_mean` should be of order **0.1 and below 1.0**, instead of 6.416. This is an expectation for a fresh critic, not a reason to reset a trained checkpoint.
+
+The task outcome to improve is final **`eval/et_test`**, currently **0.04333**. I expect recovery to at least the historical starting neighborhood, approximately **0.08**, with a working forecast around **0.10**; validation should recover toward or above **0.06**. Those are prospective estimates, not measured results or guaranteed thresholds. The system's full rerun must determine whether held-out health is restored. A reduced warmup loss alone will not establish that result.
*** End Patch"));
